description: Report rules for win11-timeline-builder (Phase 3). Data only; no code. Keyword lists (attacker tools, LOLBins, staging folders, download/AMSI/credential patterns) live ONLY in this file, never as literals in .ps1 files, because Defender's AMSI blocks PowerShell code that holds attacker-tool names. Findings are leads to review, not verdicts. Patterns are case-insensitive .NET regex; condition fields in a match object are ANDed; {{list:<name>}} expands to an escaped alternation.

rules.title: An event log was cleared
rules.why: Someone erased a Windows event log. Clearing logs is a common way to hide what happened, so the gap itself is a lead.
rules.technical: Security 1102 (audit log cleared) or System 104 (a named log cleared). The ClearedBy account and the time bound how far the surviving record reaches.
rules.nextSteps: Note which log and when, and who cleared it. Compare the first surviving event of that log with the clear time to size the gap. Cross-check other artifacts (USN, MFT, registry) for activity in the blind window.
rules.falsePositives: Administrators and some backup or imaging tools clear logs on purpose; a fresh install or a lab reset also clears logs.

rules.title: The audit policy was changed
rules.why: Windows was told to record less (or more) about what happens on the machine. Turning auditing off is a way to go quiet.
rules.technical: Security 4719. 'Success removed' or 'Failure removed' for a subcategory means that auditing was weakened; changes clustered in time often bracket other activity.
rules.nextSteps: Read which subcategories changed and in which direction. A removal right before other events is more interesting than routine policy management.
rules.falsePositives: Group Policy refreshes, security-baseline tooling, and ordinary administration change audit settings.

rules.title: The Event Log service was disabled
rules.why: The service that records Windows event logs was set not to start. With it off, almost nothing is logged.
rules.technical: System 7040 changing the EventLog service start type to disabled. Legitimate software almost never does this.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the service state and the account that made the change, and treat events after it as under-recorded.
rules.falsePositives: Very rare; some aggressive 'debloat' or privacy scripts disable logging.

rules.title: Antivirus flagged a high-severity threat: {{group}}
rules._notDescription: Test files are recognised by the threat name only, not by a folder name in the path that DetectionHistory rows append.
rules.why: The antivirus named a serious threat. These verdicts are the highest-confidence signal in the collection and set the times to look around.
rules.technical: Microsoft Defender detection across its channels (Operational log 1116/1117, defender_detections.csv, DetectionHistory, MPLog) with SeverityID High/Severe or a high-risk family name. The same detection can appear from several sources; they share the threat name.
rules.nextSteps: Find the file or command that was flagged and where it came from. Check whether the action succeeded (quarantine/remove) or failed, and look at activity in the minutes before the detection.
rules.falsePositives: Security tooling, offensive-security training material, and some admin scripts trigger high-severity names; confirm the actual file before concluding.

rules.title: Antivirus flagged malware: {{group}}
rules.why: The antivirus flagged something it considers malware, below its top severity. Still worth confirming.
rules.technical: Microsoft Defender detection rows that are not high-severity, not a PUA, and not a test file.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the flagged file and its origin; decide whether it is a real detection or a benign item.
rules.falsePositives: Low-severity or heuristic detections are more prone to false positives.

rules.title: Antivirus test file detected (EICAR): {{group}}
rules.why: The EICAR antivirus test file was detected. EICAR is a harmless industry-standard string used to check that antivirus works; by itself it is not malware, but someone put it there.
rules.technical: A Defender detection whose threat name contains EICAR. Often used to verify detection, or dropped during testing.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm who created the EICAR file and why. Treat as a test artifact unless its presence is unexplained.
rules.falsePositives: Expected whenever antivirus is deliberately tested.

rules.title: Antivirus could not remove a threat: {{group}}

match.description: ^Defender (?:action failed on threat|critical error acting on threat): (?<key>[^ |]+)

rules.why: The antivirus found a threat but failed to quarantine or remove it, so it may still be on the machine.
rules.technical: Microsoft Defender 1008/1118 (action failed) or 1119 (critical error while acting on a threat). The file may be locked, in use, or protected by the malware itself.
rules.nextSteps: Find the file named in the detection, check whether it is still present, and look for what kept it in place (a running process, a service or a scheduled task).
rules.falsePositives: A file on a read-only or network location, or one locked by a backup, can make the action fail without anything malicious keeping it.

rules.title: Antivirus flagged a potentially unwanted application
rules.why: Software the antivirus considers unwanted (adware, bundled tools) was seen. Usually not an attack, but sometimes a foothold.
rules.technical: Defender PUA/PUADlManager detections. PUA protection catching toolbars, miners or riskware.
rules.nextSteps: Decide whether the application was installed knowingly.
rules.falsePositives: Many legitimate admin and network tools are classed as PUA.

rules.title: Third-party antivirus reported a threat
rules._anyOf: The threat words are looked for after the provider name, so a product called 'Anti-Virus' does not count as a detection.
rules.why: A non-Microsoft antivirus product logged a detection or a blocked threat. These are high-confidence signals about what the product saw.
rules.technical: Parsed Symantec, Sophos, McAfee or ESET local logs, and antivirus events of about 25 other products (from the Application log or the product's own event log) whose text names a threat. Routine scans and updates are not kept by the builder.
rules.nextSteps: Read the threat name and the file or process involved; correlate with Defender and the rest of the timeline.
rules.falsePositives: Blocked-but-would-allow (audit) rules and test files appear here too.

rules.title: Third-party antivirus logged an error or warning
rules.why: A non-Microsoft antivirus product logged an error or warning that names no threat, such as a failed update or a stopped component.
rules.technical: Critical, Error and Warning events of a third-party antivirus product (Application log or the product's own log) without a threat word in the text.
rules.nextSteps: Check whether protection was degraded at the time (stopped components, failed updates) and whether that lines up with other leads.
rules.falsePositives: Update and licensing errors are common and usually harmless.

rules.title: Antivirus real-time protection was turned off

match.description: real-time protection (disabled|turned off)|scanning for (viruses|spyware and unwanted software) disabled

rules.why: Live antivirus scanning was switched off. Attackers disable protection before running tools; it is rarely off by accident.
rules.technical: Defender 5001/5010/5012 or an MPLog RTPStatus transition to 0. Real-time, behavior or on-access monitoring disabled.
rules.nextSteps: Find out when protection went off and back on, and what ran in that window.
rules.falsePositives: Some installers and troubleshooting steps briefly disable protection; a competing antivirus turns Defender off.

rules.title: Antivirus tamper protection was turned off or blocked a change
rules._anyOf: 5013 (Tamper Protection blocked a change); an MPLog state change, or a 5007 change of Features\TamperProtection, that ends in an off state (0x0 or 0x4). Turning it on is not flagged.
rules.why: The antivirus's tamper protection was turned off, or it blocked an attempt to change protected antivirus settings. Either can be a step toward disabling protection.
rules.technical: Defender 5013 (Tamper Protection blocked a change), or a Tamper Protection state that ends off (0x0 or 0x4) in the MPLog support log or a 5007 configuration change of Features\TamperProtection.
rules.nextSteps: Check what change was attempted or when protection was turned off, and whether exclusions or protection settings changed around the same time.
rules.falsePositives: Enterprise management and legitimate reconfiguration can toggle it.

rules.title: A high-risk antivirus exclusion was set
rules.why: The antivirus was told to ignore a whole drive, a folder any user can write to, a script engine, or all programs of a type. That can blind it to malware placed there.
rules.technical: A Defender exclusion covering a drive root, a user-writable folder itself (Downloads, Users\Public, PerfLogs, the Recycle Bin, a Temp folder), a scripting/LOLBin process (by name or full path), or an executable/script extension.
rules.nextSteps: Check who added the exclusion and what now runs inside it. A broad exclusion added before other activity is a strong lead.
rules.falsePositives: Developers and some products exclude build folders or their own binaries; confirm intent.

rules.title: Antivirus exclusions were added or changed
rules.why: The antivirus was told to skip certain folders, files or programs. Legitimate admins do this, but so do attackers to hide their tools.
rules.technical: Defender exclusion rows from the Operational log, MPLog, or the registry. The triage collector's own temporary exclusion of its output folder (TriageCollection_<date>_<time>) is allowlisted when it is added or removed; one still in effect after a collection is listed. Each exclusion is a place antivirus no longer looks.
rules.nextSteps: Review each excluded path or process and whether anything of interest sits inside it.
rules.falsePositives: Security, forensic and backup tools, and developers, commonly add exclusions.

rules.title: A security product reported it was off
rules.why: Windows Security Center recorded that an antivirus or firewall product reported itself as off, snoozed or expired.
rules.technical: SecurityCenter event 15 with a product state other than ON, for a product other than Microsoft Defender (see AV-DEFENDER-PRODUCT-OFF).
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the product and the period it was not protecting the machine.
rules.falsePositives: A product being replaced, updating, or legitimately snoozed.

rules.title: Windows Security Center reported Microsoft Defender as off
rules.why: Windows Security Center recorded Microsoft Defender as off, snoozed or expired. This is normal when another antivirus takes over, and a lead when none did.
rules.technical: SecurityCenter event 15 for Microsoft Defender with a state other than ON. Defender's own real-time protection switch-offs are AV-RTP-OFF (High).
rules.nextSteps: Check whether another antivirus product reported ON at about the same time; if none did, find out why Defender was off and what ran meanwhile.
rules.falsePositives: Installing a third-party antivirus makes Windows report Defender as off; so does an expired or snoozed state during setup.

rules.title: An attack surface reduction rule blocked something: {{group}}
rules.why: A Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction rule blocked a risky action, such as reading passwords from memory or an Office document starting a program.
rules.technical: Defender 1121 (an ASR rule in block mode stopped an action). The rule name says what was blocked; Details name the process and the file or command. Audit-mode events (1122) are not flagged.
rules.nextSteps: Read which process triggered the rule and what it tried to do, and whether the same process did anything else around that time.
rules.falsePositives: Some business applications and add-ins trip ASR rules during normal use.

rules.title: Antivirus detection history was deleted by a user
rules.why: Someone deleted Microsoft Defender's list of past detections. That hides what the antivirus had found.
rules.technical: Defender 1013 that is not the service's own daily retention purge (the builder labels those 'purged by retention'). DeletedBefore shows how far the deletion reached.
rules.nextSteps: Check who deleted the history and look for detections in other sources (Operational log, MPLog, DetectionHistory) before that time.
rules.falsePositives: Users and administrators sometimes clear the history after cleaning up a known detection.

rules.title: A security service crashed or was disabled
rules.why: An antivirus, endpoint-protection or monitoring service crashed or was set not to start. Attackers stop these services so their tools are not seen.
rules.technical: System 7034 (service terminated unexpectedly) for a security product, or 7040 changing a security service (WinDefend, Sense, Sysmon, an EDR agent) to disabled. Service stops logged as 7036 are not flagged: product updates restart these services routinely.
rules.nextSteps: Check how long the service was down, whether it was restarted, and what ran in that window.
rules.falsePositives: Product bugs, updates and uninstalls crash or disable security services without an attack.

rules.title: A new local account was created: {{group}}
rules._escalate: Same account: the 4720's AccountSID equals the 4732's MemberSID. The Administrators group is matched by its SID, which is the same in every Windows language.
rules.why: A new user account was created on the machine. Attackers add accounts to keep access; it rises to a strong lead if the same account was then made an administrator.
rules.technical: Security 4720. Escalates to High when the same account (by SID) is added to the local Administrators group (S-1-5-32-544) within an hour.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the account was created on purpose and by whom. Check its group memberships and first logon.
rules.falsePositives: Provisioning, new-employee setup and some software create accounts.

rules.title: An account with a name ending in $ was created: {{group}}
rules.why: A user account was created with a name ending in $, which makes it look like a computer account and hides it from some lists. That is a known trick to keep a hidden way in.
rules.technical: Security 4720 (a user account) whose name ends in '$'. Computer accounts are created with 4741, not 4720, so a 4720 with a '$' name is unusual.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the account, who created it, its group memberships and whether it has logged on.
rules.falsePositives: Rare; a few provisioning scripts name service accounts this way.

rules.title: An account was added to a privileged group: {{group}}

anyOf.description: group: (?:Remote Desktop Users|Backup Operators|Domain Admins|Enterprise Admins)

rules.why: A user was added to a powerful group such as Administrators. That grants control of the machine and is a common way to keep access.
rules.technical: Security 4728/4732/4756 adding a member to Administrators (S-1-5-32-544) or another high-privilege group.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the change was authorized, and check what the added account did afterwards.
rules.falsePositives: Legitimate administration and onboarding add users to these groups.

rules.title: An account's password was reset: {{group}}
rules._severity: Info, not the plan's Medium (P3): creating an account (net user /add, the Settings app) also logs a 4724 for the new account, so every new account would give a second lead.
rules.why: Someone reset another account's password. With administrator rights this takes over the account without knowing its old password.
rules.technical: Security 4724 (an attempt to reset an account's password). The subject (User) is the account that did it; Details name the target. Creating an account in the Windows settings also logs a reset right after the 4720.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the reset was expected and who did it, and check the target account's logons afterwards.
rules.falsePositives: Helpdesk resets, and setting the first password of a new account, log this event.

rules.title: An account was locked out: {{group}}
rules.why: An account was locked after too many wrong passwords. Usually a user mistyping, sometimes password guessing.
rules.technical: Security 4740. CallerComputer in Details names the computer the failed attempts came from.
rules.nextSteps: Look at the failed logons (4625) before the lockout and where they came from.
rules.falsePositives: Mistyped or stale saved passwords lock accounts all the time.

rules.title: A burst of failed logons from one source
rules._maxFindings: An internet-facing machine under password spraying can see thousands of sources: the worst few are separate leads, the rest one folded lead.
rules.why: Many passwords were tried quickly from one place, which looks like password guessing. It becomes a strong lead if a successful logon from the same place soon follows.
rules.technical: Ten or more Security 4625 failures from one source within five minutes. Escalates to High when a 4624 success from the same address follows within ten minutes.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the source address and the targeted accounts; confirm whether any logon finally succeeded.
rules.falsePositives: A user with a wrong saved password, a broken service account, or a scanner can produce failures without an attack.

rules.title: Remote Desktop logon from an external address

match.description: RemoteInteractive \(RDP\)|Remote Desktop Services: session (?:logon succeeded|reconnection succeeded)|RDP user authentication succeeded

rules.why: Someone signed in over Remote Desktop from an address that is not on the local network. Internet-facing RDP is a frequent way in.
rules.technical: A type-10 (RemoteInteractive) 4624, a TerminalServices LocalSessionManager logon, or a RemoteConnectionManager 1149 whose source IP is not private or loopback.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the source address and account, and whether the access was expected. Check what ran during the session.
rules.falsePositives: Legitimate remote work over a jump host or published RDP; a VPN that assigns public-looking addresses.

rules.title: Remote Desktop logon over loopback (possible tunnel)

match.description: RemoteInteractive \(RDP\)|Remote Desktop Services: session (?:logon succeeded|reconnection succeeded)|RDP user authentication succeeded

rules.why: A Remote Desktop logon came from the machine itself (127.x). That usually means the connection was tunnelled in through another channel to hide its real origin.
rules.technical: An RDP logon whose recorded source is loopback, a hallmark of SSH or other port forwarding of RDP.
rules.nextSteps: Look for the tunnel: a listening port forwarder, SSH, or a remote-access tool active at the same time.
rules.falsePositives: Some local testing and nested-session setups connect to 127.0.0.1 on purpose.

rules.title: Weak NTLMv1 authentication was used
rules.why: The machine used an old, weak logon protocol (NTLMv1) that is easy to crack or relay. Attackers force it to capture credentials.
rules.technical: A 4624 with LmPackageName 'NTLM V1', or an NTLM Operational event marked NTLMv1.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the account and the peer that negotiated NTLMv1, and whether a downgrade was forced.
rules.falsePositives: Legacy devices and old applications still use NTLMv1.

rules.title: A session was reconnected from a client
rules._severity: Info, not the plan's Medium (P5): reconnecting to one's own disconnected session is everyday use, and the rule cannot tell a hijack from it.
rules.why: An existing desktop session was reconnected from another client. Usually normal, occasionally session hijacking.
rules.technical: Security 4778 that carries a client name or address.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the client and account match the expected user.
rules.falsePositives: Everyday reconnecting to a disconnected RDP session.

rules.title: An account used another account's credentials
rules._match: The subject (User) of the routine logon-time events is the machine account (HOST$) and their target is a Window Manager or Font Driver Host session account; both are left out.
rules.why: A signed-in user supplied a different account's user name and password (runas). Normal for admins, sometimes used to move with stolen credentials.
rules.technical: Security 4648 from a human account: machine accounts (names ending in $), NT AUTHORITY accounts, and the Window Manager / Font Driver Host logons Windows makes at every sign-in are filtered out.
rules.nextSteps: Check which target account and server were used, and whether the pairing is expected.
rules.falsePositives: Administrators routinely runas; scheduled installs and scripts do too.

rules.title: A service was installed to run a command or from an unusual path: {{group}}
rules.why: A Windows service was set up to run a command line, a built-in Windows tool, or a program in a user or shared folder, instead of a normal installed program. That is a common way to run code with full control of the machine and keep it running.
rules.technical: System 7045 or Security 4697 whose ImagePath contains an inline cmd (also cmd /Q /c and %COMSPEC%, as remote-execution tools write it) or PowerShell command, a LOLBin, a path on an ADMIN$ share, or a program under a user-writable folder, \Users\ or \ProgramData\ (Defender's own platform folder excepted). The PsExec service is PERSIST-SERVICE-PSEXEC.
rules.nextSteps: Read the full ImagePath and account, confirm the service is unexpected, and look at what it launched.
rules.falsePositives: A few legitimate products install helper services with script-like paths or under ProgramData.

rules.title: The PsExec remote-execution service was installed
rules.why: The PsExec remote-execution service was installed, which means someone ran commands on this machine from another computer (or from this one as SYSTEM).
rules.technical: System 7045 or Security 4697 for the PSEXESVC (PsExec) or PAExec service. PsExec copies the service to ADMIN$ and runs the requested command through it.
rules.nextSteps: Find who ran it and from where (logons and network shares around the install time), and what commands it ran.
rules.falsePositives: Administrators and incident responders use PsExec for remote administration.

rules.title: A remote-access tool was installed as a service

match.description: ^(New service installed|Service registry key last modified)

rules.why: A remote-control product was installed as a service. Attackers often bring their own remote-access tool to keep a way back in.
rules.technical: A service whose name or ImagePath matches a known remote-access product.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the tool was installed by IT and is expected on this machine.
rules.falsePositives: Many organisations use these tools for legitimate remote support.

rules.title: A scheduled task runs a suspicious command
rules._anyOf: A task with one action is written 'Command=<program> | Arguments=<arguments>', so the patterns may cross into Arguments. The encoded switch is any abbreviation of -EncodedCommand (-e, -ec, -en, -enc, ...) followed by base64.
rules.why: A scheduled task was set to run an encoded or downloaded command, which is how attackers make code run again and again on a timer.
rules.technical: A task (TaskScheduler 106/140, Security 4698/4702, scheduled_tasks.csv, or TaskCache) whose action contains an encoded command, a download cradle, or mshta/regsvr32 fetching a URL.
rules.nextSteps: Read the task action and trigger, confirm it is unexpected, and check whether it ran.
rules.falsePositives: Some management and update tasks use PowerShell with a URL; read the command before concluding.

rules.title: A scheduled task runs a program from a user folder: {{group}}
rules.why: A scheduled task runs a program kept in a download, temp or shared folder rather than a normal install location. That placement is typical of planted code.
rules.technical: A task whose action path is under Downloads, Users\Public, PerfLogs, the Recycle Bin or a Temp folder, or a program directly in the ProgramData root.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the program and the task are expected; inspect the program file itself.
rules.falsePositives: Some installers and updaters run from Temp or keep a helper in ProgramData.

rules.title: A hidden scheduled task was found: {{group}}
rules.why: A scheduled task was hidden so that it does not show in Task Scheduler or schtasks, yet it still runs. Hiding a task is a deliberate evasion step.
rules.technical: A TaskCache\Tree entry with no SD value (the Tarrask technique), which the normal tools will not list.
rules.nextSteps: Read the task action and author, and treat the task as attacker-controlled until shown otherwise.
rules.falsePositives: Rare; a few tools and corrupt task states can leave a task without a security descriptor.

rules.title: An autostart entry runs a suspicious command
rules.why: A program that starts automatically at logon was set to run an encoded or downloaded command. That is a classic way to keep malicious code running.
rules.technical: A Run/RunOnce value or a Shell-Core logon command containing an encoded command (any abbreviation of -EncodedCommand followed by base64), a download cradle, or mshta/regsvr32 fetching a URL.
rules.nextSteps: Read the full command and confirm it is unexpected.
rules.falsePositives: A few legitimate programs use command-line autostart entries.

rules.title: An autostart entry points into a user folder
rules.why: A program set to start at logon lives in a download, temp or shared folder instead of a normal install location. That placement is typical of planted code.
rules.technical: A Run/RunOnce value whose command path is under Downloads, Users\Public, PerfLogs, the Recycle Bin or a Temp folder, or a program directly in the ProgramData root. Programs under AppData\Roaming and AppData\Local are not flagged: many legitimate applications autostart from there.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the autostart program is expected and inspect the file it points to.
rules.falsePositives: Some installers leave a one-time RunOnce entry pointing into Temp.

rules.title: A script was placed in a Startup folder
rules.why: A script file sits in a Startup folder, so Windows runs it every time a user signs in. Malware uses this simple way to start again; ordinary programs put shortcuts there instead.
rules.technical: A Win32_StartupCommand entry from a Startup folder (Location Startup or Common Startup) whose command is a script, or an MFT record of a script created in a Start Menu\Programs\Startup folder. Shortcuts (.lnk) are not flagged.
rules.nextSteps: Read the script, find when and by whom it was created, and whether it ran.
rules.falsePositives: Some users and IT departments use logon scripts in the Startup folder.

rules.title: A WMI event subscription that runs code
rules.why: A WMI subscription was set up to run a command or script when something happens on the machine. This is a stealthy way to keep code running that survives reboots.
rules.technical: A permanent WMI event subscription bound to a CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer. The built-in SCM Event Log consumer is allowlisted.
rules.nextSteps: Read the filter query and what the consumer runs; confirm it is not a known product.
rules.falsePositives: A few management and monitoring products use WMI consumers.

rules.title: An Image File Execution Options debugger was set
rules.why: Windows was told to launch another program in place of a given one. Attackers use this to run their code when a common program (or an accessibility key) starts.
rules.technical: An Image File Execution Options Debugger value. On an accessibility program it runs at the logon screen as SYSTEM.
rules.nextSteps: Read which program is hijacked and what the debugger runs.
rules.falsePositives: Developers set debuggers on their own programs; a few tools use GlobalFlag/IFEO legitimately.

rules.title: A SilentProcessExit monitor was set
rules.why: Windows was told to launch a program (or dump memory) whenever another program exits. This can run attacker code or capture credentials from a target process.
rules.technical: A SilentProcessExit entry that is active (MonitorProcess with ReportingMode 0x1, or a dump with 0x2, and the IFEO GlobalFlag set).
rules.nextSteps: Read the monitored program and what is launched or dumped.
rules.falsePositives: Rare; some crash-handling tools use it.

rules.title: A Winlogon startup value was changed
rules.why: A core logon setting (the shell or user-init program) was changed from its default, which makes extra code run at every logon.
rules.technical: A non-default Winlogon Shell, Userinit or Taskman value.
rules.nextSteps: Compare the value with the Windows default and identify the added program.
rules.falsePositives: A few kiosk and shell-replacement setups change these on purpose.

rules.title: AppInit_DLLs was set
rules.why: A DLL was set to load into many programs through the old AppInit mechanism, a way to run code broadly across the system.
rules.technical: A non-empty AppInit_DLLs value (native or Wow6432Node). Ignored when Secure Boot is on.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the DLL and confirm it is from a trusted product.
rules.falsePositives: A few legacy products still use AppInit_DLLs.

rules.title: A non-default LSA package was added
rules.why: A custom authentication or password-notification module was added to the part of Windows that handles logons. This can capture passwords or run code with high privilege.
rules.technical: A non-default entry in LSA Authentication, Notification or Security Packages.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the DLL and confirm it is a known security product.
rules.falsePositives: Some endpoint and single-sign-on products add LSA packages.

rules.title: Windows was set to keep clear-text passwords in memory
rules.why: A setting was turned on that makes Windows keep clear-text passwords in memory, where a tool can read them. Attackers flip this before dumping credentials.
rules.technical: WDigest UseLogonCredential set to 1.
rules.nextSteps: Check when the value was set and whether credential-dumping activity followed.
rules.falsePositives: Very rare on modern Windows; some legacy compatibility needs it.

rules.title: A browser extension was loaded from the command line
rules.why: A browser extension was loaded with a command-line switch (--load-extension) instead of being installed. Malware starts the browser this way to slip in an extension that steals data.
rules.technical: A Chromium extension whose install location is CommandLine (manifest location 8).
rules.nextSteps: Find what launched the browser with --load-extension (a shortcut, a task or a Run key), and read the extension's code and permissions.
rules.falsePositives: Extension developers and some test automation load extensions this way.

rules.title: A browser extension was installed outside the store
rules.why: A browser extension came from an unpacked folder, a local policy or a registry entry instead of the browser's store. That is how unwanted or malicious extensions are often pushed.
rules.technical: A Chromium extension whose install location is Unpacked, ExternalPolicy or ExternalRegistry. Extensions force-installed from the store by enterprise policy (ExternalPolicyDownload) are not flagged.
rules.nextSteps: Read the extension's permissions and path, and confirm it was installed knowingly.
rules.falsePositives: Developers load unpacked extensions; software vendors install companion extensions through the registry.

rules.title: A custom browser search engine was added or changed
rules.why: A non-standard search engine was added to the browser. Software that writes this can redirect searches, a common adware or hijack behaviour.
rules.technical: A Chromium keywords entry of kind Custom (added or edited by the user or by software writing to Web Data).
rules.nextSteps: Check the search URL template and whether the user added it.
rules.falsePositives: Users add custom search engines themselves.

rules.title: The Windows firewall was turned off or reset
rules.why: The firewall was switched off, wiped, or reset, which can open the machine to remote access.
rules.technical: A Windows Firewall profile/global setting change that disables the firewall, deletes all rules, or resets to defaults.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm who made the change and whether inbound access was opened at the same time.
rules.falsePositives: Troubleshooting and some imaging steps reset the firewall.

rules.title: PowerShell ran an encoded command
rules.why: PowerShell was run with its command hidden as encoded text. This is common in attacks to obscure what the command does, though admins and installers use it too.
rules.technical: A PowerShell invocation with -EncodedCommand or any abbreviation of it (-e, -ec, -en, -enc, ...) followed by base64, in a PowerShell 400 event (the builder decodes it into the EncodedCommand detail), a process-creation event (4688, Sysmon 1), the PSReadLine history or the Run dialog.
rules.nextSteps: Read the decoded command. Judge it by what it actually does, not by the encoding alone.
rules.falsePositives: Microsoft tooling, CI systems, and many installers use -EncodedCommand for ordinary tasks.

rules.title: A command downloaded code and ran it
rules._anyOf: High needs a download method and Invoke-Expression (iex) in the same row; a download alone is EXEC-PS-DOWNLOAD-FILE (Medium).
rules.why: A command downloaded code from the internet and ran it straight away. That pattern is how a lot of malware gets its next stage onto the machine, including fake 'paste this into Run' prompts.
rules.technical: A command line, script block, PSReadLine line or Run-dialog entry with a download method (DownloadString, Invoke-WebRequest/iwr, Invoke-RestMethod/irm, Net.WebClient, curl, ...) and Invoke-Expression (iex).
rules.nextSteps: Find the URL fetched and what the downloaded code did; check for files, tasks or connections created right after.
rules.falsePositives: Some package-manager installers (for example Chocolatey's) are started this way.

rules.title: A command downloaded a file from the internet
rules._match: Rows that also run the download (iex) are EXEC-PS-DOWNLOAD; certutil/bitsadmin with a URL are EXEC-LOLBIN-URL.
rules.why: A command downloaded a file from the internet with a scripting method. Attackers fetch their tools this way, but so do many admin scripts.
rules.technical: A command line, script block, PSReadLine line or Run-dialog entry with a download method (DownloadString, DownloadFile, Invoke-WebRequest/iwr, Invoke-RestMethod/irm, Net.WebClient, Start-BitsTransfer) and no Invoke-Expression.
rules.nextSteps: Find the URL and the file saved, and whether that file then ran.
rules.falsePositives: Setup, update and monitoring scripts download files routinely.

rules.title: A built-in Windows program was pointed at a web address
rules.why: A built-in Windows program such as mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 or certutil was told to load something from a web address. Attackers use these trusted programs to fetch and run code, for example through fake 'press Win+R and paste' prompts.
rules.technical: A command line, script block, PSReadLine line or Run-dialog (RunMRU) entry in which a LOLBin (mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, certutil, bitsadmin, msiexec and others in the lolbins list) is followed by an http(s) URL. rundll32 url.dll/ieframe.dll URL handlers, which open links in the browser, are left out.
rules.nextSteps: Find the URL and what it served, and look for processes, files and connections right after.
rules.falsePositives: Some installers run msiexec or certutil against a vendor URL.

rules.title: PowerShell used an AMSI bypass or a credential tool
rules.why: A command was seen that disables antivirus script scanning, or that steals passwords from memory. Both are strong signs of an attack rather than administration.
rules.technical: A command line (4688, Sysmon 1), script block or command history entry matching a known AMSI-bypass pattern or a known credential-dumping function. Sysmon image-load rows are not checked: loading a DLL is not a command.
rules.nextSteps: Read the full command, and check for antivirus detections or credential access around the same time.
rules.falsePositives: Offensive-security training and red-team material contain these patterns.

rules.title: A command turned off antivirus protection or added an exclusion
rules.why: A command was seen that switches off Microsoft Defender protection or tells it to ignore a folder, program or file type. Attackers do this right before running their tools.
rules.technical: Set-MpPreference or Add-MpPreference with a -Disable... switch set to true, or with an -Exclusion... parameter, in a command line, script block or command history.
rules.nextSteps: Read the full command and who ran it, and check the matching Defender configuration events (5001, 5007) and what ran afterwards.
rules.falsePositives: Deployment and developer scripts add exclusions; the triage collector adds one for its own output folder while it runs (that script block may be logged).

rules.title: PowerShell 2.0 was started (possible downgrade)
rules.why: The old PowerShell version 2 was started on a modern system. Attackers do this because version 2 skips the newer logging and script scanning.
rules.technical: A classic PowerShell 400 event with EngineVersion 2.0.
rules.nextSteps: Check why version 2 was invoked and what it ran; version 2 leaves little other evidence.
rules.falsePositives: A few legacy applications still request the version 2 engine.

rules.title: A BITS transfer fetched a program from a numeric IP address: {{group}}
rules.why: A background download fetched a program or script from a bare internet IP address. Malware uses this to bring in its tools; legitimate software downloads programs from named sites.
rules.technical: A BITS 59/60 transfer whose URL host is a public IPv4 literal and whose path ends in an executable or script extension.
rules.nextSteps: Find the file it saved, whether it ran, and which job or process asked for the download (BITS 3).
rules.falsePositives: Rare; some appliances and internal update servers are addressed by IP.

rules.title: A BITS transfer used a numeric IP address: {{group}}
rules.why: A background download used a bare internet IP address instead of a web site name. Malware often uses raw IPs for its download servers; Windows Update and most software use names.
rules.technical: A BITS 59/60 transfer whose URL host is a public IPv4 literal (private and loopback ranges are EXEC-BITS-PRIVATEIP; programs and scripts are EXEC-BITS-RAWIP-EXE). One lead per address.
rules.nextSteps: Check the IP and the file saved, and whether the file then ran.
rules.falsePositives: Some content-delivery and internal systems use raw IPs.

rules.title: A BITS transfer used a private IP address: {{group}}
rules.why: A background download came from a private (local-network) IP address. Usually an internal update server, occasionally a staging host inside the network.
rules.technical: A BITS 59/60 transfer from 10/8, 172.16/12 or 192.168/16, for example a WSUS server addressed by IP.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the address is a known internal server.
rules.falsePositives: WSUS and other internal distribution servers.

rules.title: A known attacker tool ran: {{group}}
rules.why: A program whose name matches a known attacker or dual-use tool was actually run on the machine. These tools are used for credential theft, lateral movement or reconnaissance.
rules.technical: Prefetch, BAM or UserAssist evidence of execution of a listed tool. These sources show a program ran.
rules.nextSteps: Confirm the tool and who ran it; several are dual-use and may be legitimate admin tools.
rules.falsePositives: Administrators and incident responders use some of these tools (for example PsExec) legitimately.

rules.title: A known attacker tool was present: {{group}}
rules._activityTime: Amcache and ShimCache rows are dated by file times, which can be much older than any activity; they are left out of the summary's flagged-activity window.
rules.why: A file whose name matches a known attacker or dual-use tool existed on the machine, though these sources do not prove it ran.
rules.technical: Amcache or ShimCache (AppCompatCache) entry for a listed tool. These prove the file existed, not that it executed, and their times are file times.
rules.nextSteps: Check whether the file is still present, where it is, and whether execution evidence (Prefetch/BAM) also exists.
rules.falsePositives: Dual-use admin tools and cached entries from tool downloads.

rules.title: A program ran from a user folder: {{group}}
rules._groupBy: One finding per program file name (case-insensitive), so its Prefetch, BAM and UserAssist rows are one lead, not one each.
rules._stagingExec: Temp folders are left out on purpose (the plan's R13 lists them): installers unpack and run from Temp all the time, which made this rule noisy.
rules.why: A program was run from a download, Public, PerfLogs or Recycle Bin folder rather than a normal install location. Attackers commonly run their tools from these folders.
rules.technical: Execution evidence (Prefetch/BAM/UserAssist) for an executable or script under Downloads, Users\Public, PerfLogs or the Recycle Bin. Temp folders are not included: installers run from there constantly.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the program, confirm it is expected there, and inspect the file.
rules.falsePositives: Users run installers and portable apps from Downloads; this is common and benign.

rules.title: An Office application started a script interpreter
rules.why: A Word, Excel, Outlook or PowerPoint document launched a command interpreter. That is the hallmark of a malicious macro or document.
rules.technical: A 4688 or Sysmon process-creation event whose parent is an Office application and whose child is a script host or LOLBin. Needs process-creation auditing, which is often off.
rules.nextSteps: Find the document that spawned it and the command that ran.
rules.falsePositives: A few Office add-ins legitimately launch helpers.

rules.title: A risky file type was downloaded: {{group}}
rules._groupBy: One lead per file name, so a download's started and completed rows and its Mark-of-the-Web row are one lead.
rules.why: A script, shortcut or disk-image file was downloaded from the internet. These file types are a usual way malware first arrives.
rules.technical: A browser download or a Mark-of-the-Web file with a risky extension (scripts, .lnk, .hta, disk images, .iso and the like), or a browser danger-type verdict. Plain installer downloads (.exe/.msi) are not flagged here on their own.
rules.nextSteps: Check where the file came from (HostUrl/Referrer), whether antivirus flagged it, and whether it ran.
rules.falsePositives: Users download installers and tools routinely.

rules.title: Office macros were enabled on a document
rules.why: A user turned on macros (active content) for a document. Malicious documents rely on the user doing exactly this.
rules.technical: An Office TrustRecords entry showing macros were enabled for a document that is not under an email or download folder.
rules.nextSteps: Find the document and what the macro did.
rules.falsePositives: Users enable macros for legitimate business documents and templates.

rules.title: Macros were enabled on a document from email or a download
rules.why: A user turned on macros for a document that came from email or a download folder. That is the exact sequence a malicious document relies on to run its code.
rules.technical: An Office TrustRecords entry enabling macros for a document under Content.Outlook, Olk, INetCache, Downloads or Public.
rules.nextSteps: Find the message or download the document came from, and what the macro did.
rules.falsePositives: Occasionally a legitimate document arrives by email and needs macros.

rules.title: A program ran from an email attachment folder
rules.why: A program ran from the folder where Outlook stores opened attachments. Running an attachment is a leading way attacks start.
rules.technical: Execution evidence (Prefetch/BAM/UserAssist) for a file inside Content.Outlook or Olk\Attachments.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the attachment, the message it came from, and what it did.
rules.falsePositives: Rare; opening a document from an attachment can leave execution evidence for the handling application.

rules.title: Email attachments were opened
rules._groupBy: One lead for all attachment rows (the file's created and modified rows, its shortcut, recent-documents and jump-list entries), not one per row.
rules.why: Files that came in as email attachments were opened from the mail client's attachment folder. Opened attachments are a leading way attacks start.
rules.technical: The Email parser's attachment rows (classic Outlook's Content.Outlook temp folder, where a file goes when it is opened, and the new Outlook's Olk\Attachments folder, which also keeps sent and received files), and shortcut, recent-document and jump-list rows that point into those folders. Windows Mail attachments that are only stored with a message are not flagged.
rules.nextSteps: Identify each attachment and its message, and whether the file was only opened or actually ran (see the related run finding).
rules.falsePositives: Opening ordinary attachments is normal; most are benign. For the new Outlook a file in its attachment folder may only have been received.

rules.title: Files show signs of timestomping
rules._activityTime: The row time is the $STANDARD_INFORMATION Created time, the very value the rule says may be forged; it is left out of the summary's flagged-activity window.
rules._match: Only each file's 'created' row: its 'modified' row carries the same flag and would count the file twice.
rules.why: Some executable or script files have timestamps that look back-dated, a trick used to make planted files blend in with older system files.
rules.technical: MFT records flagged [SI<FN]: a $STANDARD_INFORMATION Created time on a whole second and more than a second earlier than the $FILE_NAME Created time, for an executable or script, outside the usual servicing/installer folders. One row per file (its 'created' row, at the possibly forged time); FN.Created in Details is when the file arrived.
rules.nextSteps: Treat each flagged file as a lead, not proof. Check whether the file also has execution evidence, and compare its times with nearby files.
rules.falsePositives: Installers, archive extraction and copying can set an earlier Created time legitimately; this flag is a lead only.
rules._maxEvidence: Extracted archives can flag hundreds of files; the report lists 30, and the workbook's Finding column tags them all.

rules.title: Many files were renamed to one extension at once
rules.why: A large number of files were renamed to the same new extension in a few minutes. That is what ransomware does as it encrypts files.
rules.technical: 100 or more USN 'rename new name' records to one extension within ten minutes.
rules.nextSteps: Identify the extension and the folders affected, and look for the program that did the renaming and any ransom note.
rules.falsePositives: Bulk file conversions, backups and some software updates can rename many files.

rules.title: A memory dump of LSASS may have been created
rules.why: A dump file named after LSASS was created. LSASS holds credentials, so dumping it is a direct step toward stealing passwords.
rules.technical: A USN or MFT record for a file whose name matches lsass*.dmp.
rules.nextSteps: Find the dump file and the process that created it, and check for credential-access tooling.
rules.falsePositives: Crash dumps and diagnostics can include LSASS by coincidence, but the name is distinctive.

rules.title: The Active Directory database (ntds.dit) was accessed
rules.why: The file that stores all domain accounts and password hashes was opened or copied. On a domain controller this is a classic credential-theft step.
rules.technical: An ESENT database event or file-system record naming ntds.dit (for example from ntdsutil or a volume-shadow copy).
rules.nextSteps: Confirm whether this is a domain controller, who accessed the file, and whether a copy was made.
rules.falsePositives: Legitimate domain-controller backups and maintenance touch ntds.dit.

allowlist.reason: The triage collector adds a temporary Defender exclusion for its own output folder while it runs; the builder labels its registry row, so it is not attacker activity.
The triage collector's own labelled temporary exclusion is not attacker activity.

The triage collector adds a Defender exclusion for its output folder (TriageCollection_<date>_<time>) when it starts and removes it when it finishes; the Operational log (5007) and MPLog record both. One left in effect after a collection is still listed.
The triage collector's own temporary exclusion of its output folder, added and removed during a collection.
The built-in 'SCM Event Log' WMI consumer ships with Windows (Service Control Manager); the builder marks it as the Windows default.
